name: Gyaru magazines (egg, Popteen, Ranzuki)

lead: Gyaru magazines such as egg, Popteen and Ranzuki were the main way gyaru style spread in Japan from the 1990s: they showed exaggerated makeup, dyed and styled hair, tanning, nails, fashion and where to buy items, using reader models and street snaps as the standard of looks.

For people interested in appearance, they serve as a reference for eye makeup, lashes, hair color and styling. Popteen launched in 1980 and ended in February 2023, while egg began in 1995, ended print in May 2014 and came back online in 2018.

paras: Readers followed tutorials and product pages for makeup and hair, copied outfits and styling from models and street snaps, and sometimes became reader models themselves. Today the same looks circulate through social media, and egg has been revived online and in occasional print issues.

Wikipedia notes that Popteen's diet-related advertising raised body-image concerns. Ganguro-style deep tanning, associated with the late 1990s and early 2000s, carries ordinary skin-damage risks from UV exposure.

angle.text: The magazines act as instruction and inspiration for makeup, hair color, styling and fashion. Reader models and street snaps showed achievable versions of the look.

lead: Gyaru magazines are Japanese publications that documented and spread gyaru fashion, a youth style built around heavy eye makeup, styled and bleached or brown hair, tanning and bold clothing. Egg, Popteen and Ranzuki are among the best-known titles [1][2].

Popteen was founded in 1980, passed from Fujimi Shobo to Asuka Shinsha and then to Kadokawa Haruki Corporation in 1994, and published its final issue in February 2023. It used a reader-model system and had exclusive models called Pop Models [3]. Egg launched in 1995, featured ganguro girls, makeup tips, hairstyles and street snaps from Shibuya's Center Gai, ended print on May 31, 2014, and returned online in March 2018 [4].

These magazines taught looks directly: readers learned techniques, products and styling from models whose appearance defined the era's gyaru ideal. The style has since become more diverse as social media replaced print [2].

paras: Print magazines were central to gyaru in the 1990s and 2000s, and later largely gave way to Instagram, TikTok and X [2]. Ranzuki is among the many gyaru magazine titles listed in the gyaru overview [2].

Popteen's reader model system let readers become models, and notable alumni include Moe Oshikiri, Tsubasa Masuwaka and Aki Kawamura [3]. The gyaru article notes its diet-related advertising raised body-image concerns [2].

Egg featured ganguro photos, fashion, hairstyles, mobile phones and makeup tips, with candid street shots similar to Fruits magazine. Special issues included Manba (2004) and egg's Beauty. Spin-offs included MensEGG. It ended print in 2014, attributed to gyaru's declining popularity, and returned online in 2018 with ten physical issues since [4].

Subcultures documented include kogal (uniform-inspired), ganguro (deep tan, bleached hair, pale lip and eye makeup), hime gyaru (princess-inspired) and yamanba, with a more varied, less rule-bound scene in the Reiwa era [2].
